paper_title: World Models as Native Latent Action Models

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Large and diverse video sources, such as egocentric human video and heterogeneous robot recordings, carry rich dynamics but come either without actions or without a shared action space. Latent action models (LAMs) can recover these dynamics, but they train their inverse- and forward-dynamics models (IDM, FDM) from scratch, trading off pixel reconstruction against latent capacity and accuracy. Pretrained video world models natively generate high-fidelity dynamics, yet represent them densely, entangled across all layers. Viewing the world model as a LAM, we show that these dynamics can be extracted with minimal changes to the model. Native LAM operates one pretrained video diffusion transformer as both IDM and FDM, with learnable dynamics registers as the only causal bridge between the two, and trains on counterfactual temporal pairs that differ in motion alone, so that the registers distill a video's dynamics into a compact native latent action. We further propose a pretraining paradigm for vision-language-action (VLA) policies, Pretraining Actions from World models (PAWlicy), in which Native LAM serves as a dynamics teacher on large-scale video; unlike world action models, it never generates video. Native latent actions outperform existing LAMs on the LARY benchmark in both action classification and control regression, and replay the same motion on new robots, in new scenes, and from human hands to robots, although no transfer objective is used in training. With a 3.8B model, PAWlicy reaches a 93.6% average success rate on RoboTwin 2.0 trained with domain-randomized demonstrations, the highest among VLAs. On RoboDojo, it is competitive on every dimension we evaluate, and its Precision, evaluated by us, is on par with the leading leaderboard entries. On real robots, it improves over the pi_0.5 baseline on both tasks. Both stages use only public data and a publicly released world model.

sections.title: Start
sections.content: Qinyue Li1*, Weijie Qiao1,2*, Qingyi Tao1*, Zerui Gong1, Zhe Yang2, Quanzhou Li2, Taolin Zhang2, Jinglin He1, Zhonghua Wu1, Chen Change Loy2,3 1SenseTime Research, Singapore, 2S-Lab, Nanyang Technological University, 3ACE Robotics *Equal contribution, Project lead Large and diverse video sources, such as egocentric human video and recordings from heterogeneous robots, carry rich dynamics but come either without actions or without shared action space. Latent action models (LAMs) can recover these dynamics, but they train their inverseand forward-dynamics models (IDM, FDM) from scratch, trading off pixel reconstruction against latent capacity and accuracy. Pretrained video world models natively generate dynamics and produce high-fidelity subsequent frames, yet represent them densely, entangled across the hidden states of every layer. Viewing the world model as LAM, we show that these dynamics can be extracted with minimal changes to the model. Native LAM operates one pretrained video diffusion transformer as both IDM and FDM, with learnable dynamics registers as the only causal bridge between the two, and trains on counterfactual temporal pairs that differ in motion alone, so that the registers distill videos dynamics into compact native latent action. We further propose pretraining paradigm for vision-language-action (VLA) policies, Pretraining Actions from World models (PAWlicy), in which Native LAM serves as dynamics teacher on large-scale video; unlike world action models, it generates video neither during training nor during inference. Native latent actions outperform existing LAMs on the LARY benchmark in both action classification and control regression, and replay the same motion on new robots, in new scenes, and from human hands to robots, although no transfer objective is used in training. With 3.8B model, PAWlicy reaches 93.6% average success rate on RoboTwin 2.0 trained with domain-randomized demonstrations, the highest among VLAs. On RoboDojo, it achieves competitive results on every dimension we evaluate, and its Precision, evaluated by us, is on par with the leading entries of the public leaderboard. On real robots, it improves over the π0.5 baseline on both tasks. Both stages are trained only on publicly available data on top of publicly released world model. Keywords: Latent Action Models; Video World Models; Vision-Language-Action Models; Robot Learning. Project Page: https://pawteam-eai.github.io/native-lam/

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Video is the most abundant record of how agents act in the physical world, spanning robots of many embodiments, human manipulation, and simulation. Much of it cannot serve directly as action supervision, since egocentric human video provides no robot action labels and robot datasets record actions in embodiment-specific spaces. Latent action models (LAMs) [9, 71, 94] address this gap. An inverse-dynamics model (IDM) infers latent action from an observed change, and forward-dynamics model (FDM) reproduces the change from it. The resulting shared action space is used to pretrain vision-language-action (VLA) policies [11, 20, 45, 62, 94] and to control world models [29, 30, 74]. The quality of this space, however, is limited by how it is learned. typical LAM trains its IDM and FDM from scratch (Fig. 1a), so the objective trades off pixel reconstruction against the capacity and accuracy of the latent. Training is also fragile [60, 94]. loose bottleneck can leak the future frame [71], tight one cannot describe the motion [60, 94], and in between the latent drifts toward camera motion or distractors unrelated to the agent [11, 60]. We start from simple observation. video world model is natively an FDM (Fig. 1b). Pretrained on large-scale robot and human video, it carries strong forward-dynamics prior on how scenes evolve, renders the future faithfully, and implicitly captures inverse dynamics, which world action models (WAMs) exploit to decode actions [44, 46, 95, 108]. 1 Figure 1 World models as native latent action models. (a) Existing LAMs learn an IDM and an FDM from scratch. (b) pretrained video world model is already an FDM. (c) Native LAM runs one world model in two modes, reading latent action ˆa from video and regenerating the future from ˆa. (d) Latent actions share one space and replay the same motion from edited first frames in new setups. (e) PAWlicy pretrains VLA on ˆa without reconstructing pixels. pretrained world model can thus be viewed as unified LAM whose learning signal need not be spent on rendering. Its dynamics, however, are entangled with appearance across dense hidden states, with no compact representation from which actions can be read. The challenge is to expose these dynamics natively through compact action interface. Native LAM (Fig. 1c) appends short, temporally ordered sequence of learnable dynamics registers to pretrained video diffusion transformer and runs it in two modes, with no separate encoder or decoder and the registers as the only causal bridge between them. In IDM mode, the registers read clean clip and yield the latent action. In FDM mode, the same network regenerates the future from the first frame and this latent alone, with its original flow-matching objective and no text. Training on counterfactual temporal pairs, clips that share first frame but differ in motion, forces the latent to carry the motion. We term the resulting representation native latent actions, as it is produced and consumed by the world model itself rather than an auxiliary encoderdecoder pair. Native LAM thereby condenses the thousands of high-dimensional tokens that the world model processes for clip (3,456 tokens of dimension 2,560, using Kairos 3.1 [37] as the pretrained video DiT) into 32 latent action tokens of dimension 128, without changing the network architecture or adding separate encoder or decoder. We validate native latent actions in two respects. Quantitatively, they outperform existing LAMs in both action classification and control regression on the LARY benchmark (Sec. 4.2.1). Qualitatively, latent action extracted from robot video and replayed in FDM mode from different first frame reproduces the same motion in new scene, on another robot, or with human hand (Fig. 1d), although training uses no transfer objective. Because they can be extracted from any video, native latent actions also enable new way to pretrain policies 2 (Fig. 1e). We propose Pretraining Actions from World models (PAWlicy), in which the frozen Native LAM labels large-scale robot, human, and simulated video, and VLA learns to predict these latents and to act on them. Unlike WAMs [44, 46, 95, 108], which make the policy generate appearance-dominated future video through multi-billion-parameter generator that is optimized during training and sometimes also run at inference, PAWlicy keeps the world models dynamics and discards its rendering in both phases. Teacher latents are computed once and cached, supervision is compact, and inference runs standard-size VLA. Both Native LAM and PAWlicy are trained only on publicly available datasets. On RoboTwin 2.0 [19], PAWlicy reaches 93.6% average success rate, the highest in Tab. 5, and with clean demonstrations alone it still outperforms π0.5 [64] trained with the same past frame and augmentation by 5.5 points. On RoboDojo [18], it leads the compared methods on all four dimensions we evaluate, and its Precision, evaluated by us, is on par with the leading entries of the public leaderboard. On real robot, it lifts π0.5 from 23.3% to 76.7% on stacking three blocks and from 33.3% to 90.0% on putting shoes in box. In summary, our contributions are: Native LAM, in which pretrained video world model serves as both IDM and FDM, bridged only by dynamics registers, without separate encoder or decoder. training recipe of counterfactual temporal pairs and text-free FDM mode that makes the world model rely on its latent, applied to 46 robot, human, and simulation sources. PAWlicy, VLA pretraining paradigm on native latent actions, with evidence that these latents are actioninformative and transferable and improve over π0.5 in simulation and the real world.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Latent action models. LAPO [71] and Genie [9] showed that an IDM/FDM pair trained to reconstruct future observations recovers latent action space from unlabeled video. Most later LAMs [11, 20, 30, 41, 49, 94, 97, 100] follow this recipe and train their IDM and FDM from scratch. Nikulin et al. [60] show that, with distractors, the latents tend to collapse onto pixel change. Many LAMs further constrain the latent during training. LAPA [94] and Moto [21] quantize it into tokens, RotVLA [45] models it as rotations, ALAM [78] regularizes it for composition and reversal consistency, and UniVLA [11] conditions it on language. villa-X [20] adds proprioceptive supervision, which is closest to our kinematic grounding. Latent actions serve world models. AdaWorld [29] and DreamDojo [30] use them as the control input of world models learned from unlabeled video, and LD4WAM [74] learns latent dynamics from human video and distills them from generated futures to condition world action model. In these methods the latent actions serve world model but are still extracted by separate LAM. Native LAM reverses this relation: the world model itself extracts the latent action, and its own generator is the decoder. World models for policy learning. Pretrained video generators such as Wan [83] and robot-oriented world models such as Kairos [37] encode strong dynamics priors, and several lines of work bring them into policy learning. Video-as-policy methods generate future and recover actions with an inverse-dynamics model [26, 79]. World action models train video generator and an action generator jointly, so that one model predicts both future frames and actions [8, 12, 13, 15, 40, 44, 46, 47, 53, 74, 108]; Fast-WAM [95] shows that much of their benefit comes from video co-training rather than test-time imagination; it keeps video generation as training objective and skips it at inference. Alignment methods instead supervise the policy, or its future tokens, with representations of future observationsgenerated images [103], video-model features [34], or frozen-encoder embeddings [3, 55, 66, 101, 107]. In all three, the policy is tied to dense visual targets that are dominated by appearance, which recent studies identify as source of brittleness under visual shift [55, 66]. Native LAM uses the world model differently: it distills the models dynamics into compact latent action, and PAWlicy aligns to that latent alone, so the policy neither renders pixels nor carries video backbone. Visual representations for action. Self-supervised image and video encoders [4, 75] are widely used as visual backbones for policies. LARY [59] probes such encoders and LAMs for semantic actions and low-level robot control. Encoder features are dense, with hundreds of patch tokens per frame, whereas latent action is compact bottleneck of few tokens per segment. We therefore compare with embodied LAMs under LARYs protocol and show that compact world-model-derived latent action is more action-informative than existing ones. 3 Figure 2 Training Native LAM. (a) Each video is paired with retimed copy = ϕ of the same footage that shares the first frame but not the motion. (b) In IDM mode, dynamics registers read the clean video through read-only attention mask and are projected to the latent action ˆa; on AgiBot World and DROID, kinematic head grounds ˆa in end-effector motion. (c) In FDM mode, the same DiT regenerates the future from v0 and ˆa alone, with ˆa inserted into the token sequence through the adapter MLPin, taking over the conditioning role of text, trained with its original flow-matching loss; both clips of pair share the noise and diffusion time, so only ˆa can explain their difference.

sections.title: 3 Method
sections.content: We first train Native LAM, which turns pretrained video world model into latent action model by running it in two modes linked by dynamics registers (Fig. 2; Secs. 3.1 and 3.2). The trained Native LAM then serves as frozen dynamics teacher for PAWlicy: it extracts native latent actions from mixture of robot, human, and simulated video, on which VLA is pretrained and then fine-tuned on target-robot demonstrations (Sec. 3.3).

sections.title: 3.1 Native LAM: one world model, two modes
sections.content: Preliminaries. From frames ft and ft+k without action labels, LAM learns an inverse-dynamics encoder and forward-dynamics decoder D, ˆa = E(ft, ft+k), ˆft+k = D(ft, ˆa), (1) trained so that ˆft+k matches ft+k, with bottleneck on ˆa that keeps it from copying the future. One backbone, two modes. Native LAM has no separate encoder or decoder. Both and are the same pretrained video diffusion transformer Gθ, the publicly released Kairos 3.1 4B robot world model [37], which operates on the latents of frozen video VAE: clip is encoded as = (v0, v1, . . . , vN ), where v0 encodes the first frame and each later vi short temporal segment. Gθ runs in an IDM mode and an FDM mode with shared weights, and short sequence of learnable dynamics registers is the only causal bridge between them (Fig. 2bc). IDM mode: registers read the clip. We append to the tokens of clean clip and run Gθ at τ = 0 (Fig. 2b). Under read-only attention mask (Fig. 2b, right), the registers attend to all video tokens and to one another, but no video token attends to them, so the video stream is computed exactly as in the pretrained model and the registers act purely as readers of its internal states. small output MLP (Fig. 2b) maps their final states to the latent action, ˆa = Eθ(v0:N ) = MLPout (cid:0)Gθ(v0:N , r)r (cid:1), (2) where ()r denotes the outputs at the register positions; Eθ takes the place of E(ft, ft+k) in Eq. (1). Grouped by time, ˆa forms short, temporally ordered sequence of continuous tokens. FDM mode: the world model replays the latent. The same network then generates the future from the first frame 4 and the latent action alone (Fig. 2c), taking the place of D(ft, ˆa): ˆv1:N = Dθ(v0, ˆa) = Gθ (cid:0) v0, MLPin(ˆa) (cid:1), (3) where Gθ now generates by integrating its flow from noise, and the adapter MLPin maps ˆa to the width of Gθ and replaces the text or action condition that the world model would otherwise receive. The input is thus [v0, MLPin(ˆa), vτ 1:N ] (Fig. 2c, bottom). FDM mode sees no text and no clean future, so all information about how the scene unfolds must be carried by ˆa. We train it with the backbones own flow-matching objective on the future latents (Fig. 2c, top): with ϵ (0, I), τ [0, 1], and vτ 1:N = (1 τ )v1:N + τ ϵ, Lfm = Eτ,ϵ w(τ ) (cid:13) (cid:13)uθ (cid:0) vτ 1:N , τ v0, MLPin(ˆa) (cid:1) (ϵ v1:N ) (cid:13) 2, (cid:13) (4) where uθ is the velocity predicted by Gθ and w(τ ) the backbones timestep weighting [48, 50]. Gradients flow through the generator into ˆa, the registers, and the shared weights. Reading latent action takes one forward pass on clean clip, with no denoising.

sections.title: 3.2 Making the world model rely on the latent
sections.content: Counterfactual temporal pairs. pretrained world model that sees the first frame can already imagine plausible future. Trained directly on video from its own pretraining domain, it suffers from posterior collapse: the FDM ignores the newly initialized latent pathway and leaves the registers uninformative (Sec. 4.2.4). We remove this shortcut. For each clip we draw time map ϕ and build = ϕ from the same source video, with x0 = x0 (Fig. 2a). The map ϕ holds the first frame (static), pauses mid-clip (pause), changes speed mid-clip (speed), retimes the motion toward the same endpoint (timing), or plays backward into the preceding frames or faster when the source allows. Frames are taken at native indices: nothing is interpolated, padded, or extrapolated. Both clips are read independently in IDM mode; in FDM mode they share the first frame, the context, the noise ϵ, and τ . The two generation problems are identical except for the latent, so the only way to solve both is for ˆa and ˆa to carry the difference in motion. Kinematic grounding. For AgiBot World 2026 [2] and DROID [39], the only two sources whose action labels we use, shallow kinematic head (Fig. 2b, top right) reads ˆa and predicts, for each group, end-effector waypoints at several horizons after the segment start: base-frame translation, rotation log(RtargetRstart), and gripper change. Targets are derived from measured trajectories and recomputed after the time map, so static clip has zero motion. The loss Lkin has weight λkin = 0.1, warmed up over the first 2,000 updates so that the world model shapes the registers first. All other sources are video only, without action or text labels. The full objective is LLAM = Lfm(x) + Lfm(x) + λkin 1kin (cid:3), (cid:2)Lkin(x) + Lkin(x) (5) where 1kin indicates clip from these two sources.

sections.title: 3.3 PAWlicy: pretraining actions from world models
sections.content: PAWlicy is pretraining paradigm in which the trained Native LAM acts as frozen dynamics teacher. The teacher assigns native latent actions to every video, irrespective of whether actions were recorded, and VLA is trained to predict these latents and to condition its actions on them. We instantiate the paradigm with three experts that share attention  (Fig. 3)  : vision-language model (VLM) that encodes the observation and instruction, latent action DiT that predicts native latent actions, and an action DiT that generates motor commands. Reconstructing the past to predict the future. The VLM is pretrained for vision-language understanding, and its representations are not trained to match the latent space of Native LAM. Predicting future latents directly from them asks the latent action DiT to map into this space and to forecast dynamics that have not yet been observed, all at once. We ease this by adding past latent group to the target and past frame to the input. Native LAM encodes eight groups per clip; we truncate the target ˆat to the first four, which keeps the prediction horizon of PAWlicy close to that of common VLAs: one group for the segment that has just been observed and three for the segments that follow. In addition, the VLM receives, besides the current image, past frame from the beginning 5 Figure 3 PAWlicy. frozen Native LAM labels each video window with one past and three future latent groups; 1, t, . . . , t+3 index temporal groups, each containing four video frames. Sharing attention with the VLM, the latent action DiT reconstructs the past and predicts the future, and the action DiT conditions on it to generate actions. Video without actions still trains the latent pathway. of the observed segment. Recovering the past group from the two images is an inverse-dynamics problem whose answer is contained in the input. This reconstruction objective therefore provides dense and well-posed signal that encourages the VLM output to align with the latent space, and lets the future groups, which are generated jointly with it, continue from latent anchored in what has already been observed. Beyond using the past frame for this reconstruction, the latent action DiT must also predict reliably when no past frame is available, as at the start of an episode. We therefore drop the past frame at random, and additionally at the start of an episode during fine-tuning. Architecture. The latent action DiT generates ˆat from noise while attending to the VLM tokens. The action DiT generates an action chunk at:t+K while attending, at every layer, to the VLM tokens and to the keys and values of the latent action DiT. Through this shared attention, the predicted latent conditions every action layer and serves as plan expressed in the representation of the world model. Both experts are trained with flow matching, LPAW = λ Lfm (cid:0)ˆat; ˆat (cid:1) + 1act Lfm (cid:0) at:t+K; at:t+K (cid:1), (6) where Lfm(y; y) is the flow-matching loss of Eq. (4) for prediction of the target y, and 1act indicates that action labels are used. Since every video yields latent target, egocentric human, cross-embodiment, and simulated video all contribute to the dynamics pathway, whereas action-labeled robot data additionally supervises the action DiT. The VLM is PaliGemma, initialized from the π0.5 base model [64]. The latent action DiT and the action DiT both have the architecture of the π0.5 action expert, with 18 layers of width 1024 (0.43B parameters each), so that PAWlicy has 3.78B parameters in total, against 3.35B for π0.5. At inference, both DiTs run 10 synchronous Euler flow-matching steps; at each step, the latent action DiT updates ˆat and supplies its per-layer keys and values to the action DiT. Pretraining and fine-tuning. We pretrain on this mixture and fine-tune on target-robot demonstrations with the same objective, with the frozen teacher still providing latent targets. sections.title: 4 Experiments
sections.content: We evaluate what native latent actions capture and how they transfer (Sec. 4.2), then test PAWlicy in simulation and on real robot and analyze its compute cost (Sec. 4.3).

sections.title: 4.1 Setup
sections.content: Implementation of Native LAM. Native LAM is trained on 46 video sources: real-robot datasets (65% sampling rate), human egocentric and hand-object video (30%), and simulation (5%). We use main, head, or external cameras only. Starting from the public backbone, we train for 13k iterations on 32 GPUs. Only AgiBot World 2026 and DROID provide kinematic grounding; all other data are video only, without action or text labels (Tab. 1). All human video comes from publicly released datasets, used under their licenses and the consent and de-identification procedures of their creators; we collect no new human data. Implementation of PAWlicy. PAWlicy is pretrained on 16 datasets: 12 of the Native LAM sources and four further datasets. The simulation benchmarks RoboTwin 2.0 and RoboDojo are excluded from PAWlicy pretraining. The frozen Native LAM provides latent target for every clip, and the action DiT is supervised on the robot datasets marked in Tab. 1. For robot data, the wrist-camera views of each episode are added to the VLM input. We pretrain PAWlicy for 50k iterations on 32 GPUs with global batch size of 512. Benchmarks. LARY [59] probes representations for the robot actions underlying video. For closed-loop control, RoboTwin 2.0 [19] provides 50 bimanual tasks with clean and domain-randomized scenes and tests robustness to visual variation; RoboDojo [18], recent benchmark with public leaderboard, groups 42 simulation tasks into five capability dimensions; and two tasks on real AgileX NERO robot, stacking three blocks and putting shoes in 7 Table 2 Evaluation on LARY [59] against embodied latent action models: action classification (top-1 %) and control regression (normalized MSE). We compare against π0.5 [64] and against π0.5 with the same past frame and augmentation as PAWlicy (π0.5 + past + aug.; we use the online image augmentation of PatchWAM [84]), post-trained with the same end-effector action space, data, and budget, so that the two differ only in the PAWlicy pretraining stage.

sections.title: 4.2.1 Action evaluation on LARY
sections.content: LARY [59] probes frozen representation of video for the actions it depicts, on two tracks: semantic action classification on composite human and robot sets, and regression of the underlying end-effector actions on CALVIN [56], VLABench [99], RoboCOIN [88], and AgiBot-Beta [10]. For the regression track we encode the source video segment of each sample, since Native LAM reads clips rather than frame pairs. Table 2 shows that Native LAM is the strongest latent action model on both tracks. It reaches 71.77% classification accuracy and 0.25 regression error on average, against 70.75% and 0.37 for WLA3, the best previous LAM. The margin holds on every dataset, and is largest on the real-robot sets RoboCOIN (0.36 against 0.55) and AgiBot-Beta (0.41 against 0.57). None of the four regression datasets is used to train Native LAM: AgiBot World 2026 is collected on the G2 rather than the G1 of AgiBot-Beta, so the two share no trajectories, and the other three are unseen. Native LAM stays frozen during probing.

sections.title: 4.2.2 Motion that transfers and interpolates
sections.content: During training, each latent is decoded only from the first frame of its own video. At test time, we read latent from one video in IDM mode and replay it in FDM mode from different first frame  (Fig. 4)  , changing the embodiment (a), the scene (b), the agent from human to robot hand (c), or the domain from simulation to photorealistic scene (d). In every case the generated video performs the source motion with the new agent in the new scene: the latent captures what is done, largely independently of who performs it and in which scene. Interpolation tests whether the latent space is organized by motion or by appearance. We replay (1 β)ˆastill + βˆafull, mixing the latents of still clip and full-action clip, from the same first frame  (Fig. 5)  . Each intermediate β yields one coherent motion that travels part of the way, further as β grows, whereas blending the two videos pixels superimposes static and moving arms. mixture of latents is thus an intermediate motion, not an intermediate image. 8 Figure 4 Native latent actions transfer. latent ˆa is read once from source clip (blue) in the IDM mode of Native LAM and replayed in its FDM mode from different first frame (orange), which is generated with GPT image generation from the source first frame; dotted frames are generated. The generated videos carry out the source motion with another embodiment, in another scene, from human to robot, and from simulation to photorealistic scene, although no transfer objective is used in training. Figure 5 Interpolating latents interpolates the motion. Latents read from still clip and full-action clip are blended and replayed from the same first frame. The top and bottom rows are the two source clips; the dotted frames between them are generated. Each intermediate latent yields one coherent motion that travels part of the way, further as β grows; blending pixels instead superimposes static and moving arms (red box).

sections.title: 4.2.3 Visual comparison with other LAMs
sections.content: We compare Native LAM with four other LAMs when the latent actions are decoded back into the clip they were read from, frame by frame and for the whole clip. Frame by frame, the latents of the other LAMs reconstruct large motions poorly in pixels: the arm and the banana blur or vanish during the fast transport (third frame of Fig. 6a). 9 Figure 6 Frames generated from the latent actions of different LAMs. real-robot clip of picking up banana and placing it in basket (top row) runs left to right; the first frame is real. (a) Frame by frame: every method, Native LAM included, is used as conventional LAM on frame pairs; for each two consecutive frames, it encodes the latent action between them (IDM) and generates the second frame from the real first one with its own world model (FDM), similar to teacher forcing. (b) Whole clip (autoregressive): the other LAMs generate each frame from the previously generated one with the latent action of the corresponding pair of real frames; Native LAM reads the whole clip at once in IDM mode and generates the whole clip from the real first frame in one pass in FDM mode. Native LAM reconstructs both large and small motions sharply, which we attribute to the prior of its pretrained world model, and the generated motion follows the source. For the whole clip (Fig. 6b), the frame-pair LAMs must roll out autoregressively, so their errors accumulate and within few steps the arm and the banana blur away or stop moving. Native LAM generates the clip in one pass, which these LAMs cannot do directly, and keeps the arm, the banana, and the motion intact to the end.

sections.title: 4.2.4 Counterfactual pairs prevent posterior collapse
sections.content: Without counterfactual pairs, the pretrained FDM learns to ignore the latent (Sec. 3.2). Gθ is initialized from Kairos 3.1, pretrained on large-scale robot and human manipulation video, and already predicts canonical trajectories from v0 alone, while the dynamics registers r, the output MLP, and the adapter MLPin(ˆa) start from random weights. Optimization therefore suppresses the adapter pathway instead of routing dynamics through r; gradients into vanish, and FDM rollouts become insensitive to ˆa (register bypass). The pairs remove this shortcut, since the two flow-matching targets differ only through ˆa and ˆa. The collapse appears early. Figure 7 compares two runs after 2k steps that differ only in whether counterfactual pairs are used, together with the final model at 13k steps. In the source clip the left arm grasps tissue. Without pairs, the FDM sends the arm to the cup whether the latent comes from this clip or from its still counterfactual: the latent is ignored, and the model hallucinates reach for the cup from the first frame alone. With counterfactual pairs, the still latent already yields still rollout at 2k steps, while the moving latent is not yet followed, and at 13k steps both rollouts match their sources. 10 source clip generated end frame start end w/o counterfactual pairs, 2k with counterfactual pairs, 2k with counterfactual pairs, 13k (final) grasps tissue reaches cup reaches cup grasps tissue moving source still source still reaches cup stays still stays still Figure 7 Counterfactual pairs prevent posterior collapse. latent action is read in IDM mode from source clip in which the left arm grasps the tissue (top) or from its still counterfactual, which holds the first frame (bottom), and the FDM regenerates the clip from the same start frame with shared prompt, noise, and seed. Circles mark the end pose of the arm. Trained for 2k steps without counterfactual pairs, the FDM reaches for the cup in both cases. This is posterior collapse: the FDM ignores the latent and hallucinates reach for the cup from the first frame alone. With counterfactual pairs, the same 2k steps already keep the still latent still, although the moving latent still reaches for the cup. sections.title: 4.3 PAWlicy in simulation and the real world
sections.content: Simulation. On RoboTwin 2.0, we train on clean demonstrations only (50 per task) or on clean and randomized demonstrations (50+500 per task), test on clean (c) or randomized (r) scenes, giving c2c, c2r, r2c, and r2r, and run the official 100 evaluation episodes per task. Table 3 measures the effect of PAWlicy pretraining. Trained on clean demonstrations only, PAWlicy improves over π0.5 with the same past frame and augmentation by 4.18 points in clean scenes and by 6.78 points in randomized scenes, reaching 74.02% on average against 68.54%. The gain is largest when the test scenes differ from the training scenes, consistent with latent that encodes motion rather than appearance. With randomized demonstrations added, Tab. 5 places PAWlicy among published results. It reaches 93.8% in clean and 93.4% in randomized scenes; the clean-scene result is second only to LD4WAM [74] (94.0%), and both the randomized-scene result and the average of 93.6% are the best in the table. The average exceeds the strongest VLA and world action model in the table and improves on RotVLA [45], the best previous VLA that uses latent actions, by 4.5 points, although PAWlicy generates no video in training or inference. On RoboDojo, we do not compare on Memory, which requires memory module that PAWlicy does not have. PAWlicy observes the current image and single frame from the segment that has just ended, whereas the Memory tasks require information that is no longer visible, and the entries that lead them are built for this purpose; for example, the DM0.5 team reports that initializing from their memory-pretrained model improves memory tasks [25]. Following the official setting, we fine-tune on its 3,500 released trajectories, 100 for each of the 34 training tasks plus 100 auxiliary ones (the Open tasks have no training data), and report success rates over 50 episodes per task, averaged over three seeds; as PAWlicy is not on the leaderboard, we evaluate it ourselves with the released code. PAWlicy is the best among the methods in Tab. 5 on all four dimensions despite its relatively small model size. The leading leaderboard entries [76, 91, 92] build on in-house or undisclosed pretraining data, whereas PAWlicy uses only public data; still, its Precision is on par with the leading entries. Real world. We evaluate the two tasks in Tab. 4, fine-tuning each policy on 100 demonstrations per task and evaluating it over 30 trials. The robot is an AgileX NERO with two 7-DoF arms, observed through head camera and two wrist cameras at 20 Hz. The three policies are fine-tuned with the same recipe, separately on each task, and deployed alike: each call returns 50-step action chunk that is executed in full before the next call. PAWlicy reaches 76.7% and 90.0%, against 66.7% and 80.0% for π0.5 with the same past frame and augmentation and 23.3% and 33.3% for π0.5. Similar to its advantage in Precision in simulation, PAWlicy performs more precise placement in both tasks. In stacking, PAWlicy places the cubes more precisely. In the shoe task, the failures of all three policies look alike: in most of them the right shoe does not end up flat in the box, but leans on the wall, tips onto the left shoe, or stands on its toe. PAWlicy fails in 3 of 30 trials, against 6 for π0.5 with the same past frame and augmentation and 20 for π0.5. Training and inference cost. World action models learn dynamics through multi-billion-parameter video expert, such as Wan 2.2 5B in Motus [8] and Fast-WAM [95] or Kairos 3.1 in Kairos-WAM [37], whereas PAWlicy predicts native latent actions with 0.43B latent action DiT trained from scratch. sections.title: 5 Conclusion and Future Work
sections.content: We show that pretrained video world model can serve as native latent action model. Through dynamics registers, Native LAM distills motion information entangled with appearance into compact latent that transfers across scenes and embodiments and interpolates into coherent intermediate motions. As frozen teacher, it enables PAWlicy to learn from robot, human, and simulated video without generating video during policy training or inference, improving generalist VLA in simulation and on real robot. This study establishes the paradigm on Kairos 3.1. Only two of 46 training sources provide kinematic grounding; the remainder are video-only, and the evaluation datasets contain no overlapping trajectories, indicating that the learned action structure is not simply inherited from dense action labels. The transfer experiments preserve initial geometry while varying embodiment, scene, or domain, providing controlled qualitative test of motion retention. Future work will test other video DiTs, isolate the contribution of kinematic grounding, and evaluate broader geometric changes and additional robots. As video world models improve, their internal dynamics may provide an increasingly scalable foundation for learning actions from video.
